criteria.description: Identifies the zero polynomial as the zero vector and argues closure under addition/scaling.
Gives a correct basis, e.g. {1, t, t^2}, and correctly states dim(P_2)=3.

commonErrors: Trying to verify every single axiom in exhaustive detail rather than noting they inherit directly from the real-number axioms applied coefficient-wise.
Giving a spanning set that isn't linearly independent (e.g. including a redundant polynomial) as the 'basis'.

solutions.fullSolution: Zero vector: the zero polynomial p(t)=0 (all coefficients zero). Closure: adding two polynomials of degree <=2 gives coefficients that add componentwise, still degree <=2; scaling similarly preserves degree <=2. All the abelian-group and distributive axioms reduce directly to the corresponding real-number axioms applied to each coefficient a_0,a_1,a_2 independently, so they hold automatically. A basis is {1, t, t^2}: every p=a_0+a_1t+a_2t^2 is a unique linear combination of these three, so they're linearly independent and spanning, giving dim(P_2)=3. The coordinates of p in this basis are exactly (a_0,a_1,a_2).

criteria.description: Identifies that the underlying vector/physical quantity doesn't change when you change basis, only its numeric description does.
Gives a concrete reason this matters (e.g. avoiding frame-mixing bugs, reasoning about basis-independent physical outcomes).

commonErrors: Treating this as a purely abstract/philosophical point without connecting it to a practical consequence.
Conflating change of basis with a physical rotation of the object itself (the object doesn't move; only the description changes).

solutions.fullSolution: A vector like a physical displacement or velocity is a geometric object that exists independent of how you choose to describe it numerically. Its coordinates are just a particular numeric encoding relative to a chosen basis, and change if you change the basis, even though the underlying vector doesn't. Keeping this distinction matters practically: it lets you correctly reason about which quantities are basis-independent (physical relationships, the vector itself) versus basis-dependent (a specific list of numbers), which becomes essential once multiple coordinate frames are in play (e.g. robot base frame vs. end-effector frame vs. world frame), since conflating a vector with one specific coordinate list makes it easy to silently mix up which frame a set of numbers actually belongs to.

criteria.description: Recognizes that the rows of B^-1 are exactly the dual basis 1-forms (coordinate-picking functions).
Verifies all four e-hat_i(b_j) = delta_ij relations explicitly.

commonErrors: Trying to find the dual basis via some other construction instead of recognizing the direct link to B^-1's rows.
Sign error in computing B^-1 for this particular (non-symmetric) basis matrix.

solutions.fullSolution: Coordinates c=B^-1 v satisfy c_i = e-hat_i(v) by definition, so the rows of B^-1 ARE the dual basis vectors. B=[[1,0],[1,1]] (columns b1,b2). det(B)=1*1-0*1=1. B^-1 = (1/1)*[[1,0],[-1,1]] = [[1,0],[-1,1]]. So e-hat_1=(1,0), e-hat_2=(-1,1) (as row vectors/1-forms). Check: e-hat_1(b1)=1*1+0*1=1, e-hat_1(b2)=1*0+0*1=0, e-hat_2(b1)=-1*1+1*1=0, e-hat_2(b2)=-1*0+1*1=1. All match delta_ij. (Numerically verified by direct matrix inversion while authoring this module.)

criteria.description: Correctly sets up v = sum_i c_i b_i as the matrix equation v = Bc.
Correctly solves for c by inverting B, using the fact that a basis matrix is invertible.

commonErrors: Writing v = B^{-1}c or another incorrect arrangement of the matrix equation.
Not noting that B being a basis (linearly independent columns spanning the space) is exactly what guarantees invertibility.

solutions.fullSolution: v = sum_i c_i b_i is exactly the matrix-vector product v = Bc, where B has the b_i as its columns and c is the vector of unknown coefficients. Since {b_i} is a basis, the b_i are linearly independent and span the space, which means B is a square, invertible matrix. Left-multiplying v=Bc by B^{-1} gives B^{-1}v = c, i.e. [v]_B = B^{-1}v.
